I'm Vikashni, an M.Tech student in Climate Change and Disaster Management at Anna University, with a B.E. in Geoinformatics Engineering. My interests include GIS, Remote Sensing, Google Earth Engine, Python and climate science. For NASA Space Apps 2026, I'm developing AgriResilience, NASA powered agricultural climate intelligence platform.

I'm looking for collaborators skilled in agriculture, UI/UX who are interested in building practical, data driven solutions for climate resilient agriculture
summary: AgriResilience is a screening dashboard for Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu. It combines NASA satellite rainfall, crop greenness and weather data to show where farmland may be under climate stress. The district’s nine blocks are compared with their own usual conditions for the same season. Rainfall deficit, dry spell, heat and crop greenness are kept as separate signals and a block is highlighted when several agree. The dashboard shows how much mapped farmland sits in flagged blocks. It marks crop greenness “not assessed” when too few satellite images exist, instead of showing a misleading number. Every flag has a decision trace that gives the value, the threshold and the distance to it. For the June to September 2026 monsoon, two blocks (Radhapuram and Manur) had at least 10% less rain than usual, covering about 22,500 ha (26% of mapped farmland). It is a planning aid, not a yield forecast or a drought declaration.
details:
What it does and how it works

AgriResilience is an agricultural climate stress screening dashboard for the nine blocks of Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu. It answers one practical need: where should agriculture officers look first when a season goes wrong?

A Python pipeline pulls three NASA datasets for each block:

  • NASA HLS Sentinel-2 (30 m): crop greenness (NDVI), vegetation moisture (NDMI) and the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), calculated on farmland only after masking cloud, shadow, snow and water.
  • NASA GPM IMERG V07 (about 11 km): seasonal rainfall.
  • NASA POWER: temperature and dry spells (consecutive days with under 1 mm of rain).

Farmland comes from the ESA WorldCover land-cover map, so forest and scrub are not counted as crops. Each season is compared with the same season in earlier years. Rainfall deficit, dry spell, heat and crop greenness are kept as separate signals. A block is highlighted only when several signals agree. The dashboard also reports how many hectares of mapped farmland sit in flagged blocks.

For the June to September 2026 monsoon, Radhapuram (19% below usual) and Manur (12% below) had at least 10% less rain than usual. Together they hold about 22,500 ha, or 26% of the district’s mapped farmland. Temperature was above the same season average but the temperature grid is coarse, so that signal describes the whole district rather than single blocks.

How it stays honest

  • Vegetation reliability check. A season is judged only if enough satellite images exist compared with a normal year. For 2026 there were roughly 21 images per month against a usual 208, so crop greenness is shown as “not assessed” instead of a number that could reflect missing images.
  • Decision trace. Every flag shows its value, the threshold and the distance to it. For rainfall it also shows how many millimetres would have changed the result. Manur, for example, was only about 5 mm of rain from clearing its flag.
  • Weak model not presented as an explanation. We tested whether rainfall, temperature and dry-spell anomalies explain year-to-year greenness. Out-of-sample R² was about −0.06, meaning no predictive skill. The dashboard reports this and does not present the model as an explanation.
  • No adaptive-capacity score. No irrigation data was available and missing data must not be read as low capacity. The dashboard lists the data gaps instead.

Benefits and intended impact

Block level officers and farmer groups get a traceable, plain language view of rainfall and crop conditions. The dashboard shows how far each result can be trusted and its adaptation page lists general options to discuss locally. The intended impact is better prioritisation of field visits and earlier conversations about water, crop sequence and insurance. It is a planning aid, not a yield forecast or an official drought declaration.

Tools

  • Languages and libraries: Python, pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Plotly.
  • Platforms: Google Earth Engine API and the NASA POWER API for data, Streamlit for the dashboard.
  • Hardware: no specialised hardware. The dashboard runs offline from the pipeline’s saved results.
  • Reproducibility: one command runs the pipeline, tests and dashboard and a run manifest records versions, settings and input checksums.

What is creative

The main idea is to treat uncertainty as a feature. Instead of one opaque risk score, the dashboard keeps evidence separate and refuses to judge where the data cannot support a judgment. It also explains every flag in plain terms, including how close each block was to the threshold. The optional composite index (ACSI) is labelled exploratory, with weight sensitivity tests and is not the headline result.

What the team considered

  • A low NDVI is not proof of drought, because harvested and fallow fields also look less green.
  • Rainfall and temperature grids are coarser than the blocks, so neighbouring blocks can share values.
  • Thresholds and weights are design choices not calibrated or official categories.
  • Seasons follow an assumed monsoon convention rather than a local crop calendar.
  • The farmland map is a single year (2021) and has not been checked against official crop statistics.
  • The only cross check so far is GPM against POWER monthly rainfall (r = 0.89). That is a consistency check, not independent validation. Validation against IMD data is the next step.
